analysis.one_liner: Offers every U.S. resident Medicare-style government health coverage, with drug-price negotiation and caps on out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 32 Democratic cosponsors, including two committee chairs, but never received a hearing or vote, dying in House subcommittees when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: AmeriCare would have made a public health insurance plan — Medicare's hospital and medical benefits plus prescription drugs — available to every U.S. resident starting in 2010, with automatic enrollment at birth. People with an employer plan certified as equivalent could stay out; everyone else would owe premiums on a sliding scale, with subsidies below three times the poverty line and no deductibles or coinsurance for children, pregnancy care, or low-income adults. Employers with 100 or more workers would have had to fund at least 80 percent of their employees' coverage, and the government would negotiate prescription drug prices. The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone without adequate coverage. AmeriCare entitled every U.S. resident to Medicare-style benefits plus prescription drugs starting in 2010, enrolled automatically at birth. Out-of-pocket costs were capped at $2,500 a year per person ($4,000 per family, adjusted for inflation), and families between two and five times the poverty line faced caps of 5 to 7.5 percent of income instead. Children under 24, pregnancy-related care, and people under twice the poverty line carried no deductible or coinsurance at all, and families below twice poverty paid no premium. Medicare enrollees would get the same improved cost-sharing, and providers could not bill patients above the program rate.

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident would be entitled to AmeriCare coverage effective 2010, with automatic enrollment at birth and an AmeriCare card used for identification and claims.

Benefits match Medicare's hospital and medical coverage plus a prescription drug benefit at least as rich as the 2006 standard federal-employee plan, with the Secretary required to negotiate prices with manufacturers and steer patients to cheaper therapeutic equivalents.

Annual out-of-pocket costs are hard-capped: a $350 deductible ($500 family maximum), 20 percent coinsurance, and a stop at $2,500 per person or $4,000 per family, with lower percentage-of-income caps for families between 200 and 500 percent of poverty.

Children under 24, pregnant women, and people below 200 percent of poverty pay no deductible or coinsurance and get extra benefits — well-child and preventive dental care, eyeglasses, hearing aids, and full screening-and-treatment coverage for kids.
Mental health and substance abuse treatment are covered on the same terms as medical and surgical care; recommended preventive services and family planning carry no cost-sharing.

Premiums are subsidized on a sliding scale below 300 percent of poverty (eliminated below 200 percent), employers must fund at least 80 percent of their workers' coverage, and providers are barred from billing patients above the program rate.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers would lose most of their market: AmeriCare would be the default plan, with private coverage surviving only as certified employer equivalents, optional Medicare Advantage-style plans inside the program, and tightly regulated supplemental policies. Drug makers would face government price negotiation, extended to Medicare itself. Employers with 100 or more workers would owe at least 80 percent of premium costs for employees on AmeriCare unless they already fund an equivalent plan at that share (small employers are exempt only until 2013). Individuals pay income-scaled premiums, states must keep paying their 2007 Medicaid and children's-health spending into the program, and general revenues cover the subsidies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, drug makers, and large employers

drawbacks.text: Nearly every household owes a new premium, set by the Secretary from projected coverage costs and collected through the tax system by wage withholding — a real obligation even after subsidies and employer contributions.
The employer mandate is heavy: firms with 100 or more workers must pay at least 80 percent of premium costs for employees on AmeriCare, and the exemption for smaller employers lasts only until 2013.

The financing is thin on paper: the trust fund runs on the new premiums and employer contributions plus appropriations matching the revenue they raise, with general revenues added for subsidies — no broader dedicated tax backs the full cost of covering everyone.

Providers would be paid Medicare rates with no extra billing allowed, which is less than private insurers pay today, and the bill's own surcharge on employers whose workers stay in private plans — written 'to prevent adverse selection' — shows the drafters worried the opt-out would draw healthier people into private coverage and leave the public plan with costlier patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the benefit side this was one of the most sweeping coverage guarantees ever put into a House bill: universal eligibility, hard out-of-pocket caps, free coverage for children and low-income adults, mental health parity, and government-negotiated drug prices. The costs are real but broadly spread — premiums on a sliding scale, a substantial employer mandate, continued state Medicaid spending, and general-revenue subsidies — and the design's weak points are honest ones: financing without a dedicated broad tax, and provider payment at Medicare rates with the two-tier risk of an employer-plan opt-out. It was a complete, detailed legislative draft rather than a vague statement bill; what it lacked was any committee willing to move it.

outcome.mechanism: Sent to three House committees and then parked in their subcommittees, it never got a markup, hearing, or floor vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on March 29, 2007, joined at introduction by 24 House members including Charles Rangel, George Miller, Henry Waxman, John Conyers, and Jan Schakowsky.
The Speaker referred it the same day to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — each for the portions under its jurisdiction.
Within months each committee passed it down to a subcommittee: Health on March 30, Health on April 20, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on July 9, 2007.
Cosponsorship grew to 32 members, every one of them a Democrat.
That July 2007 subcommittee referral is the last recorded action; no markup, hearing, report, or vote ever followed, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries the bill targeted: private insurers kept their market and drug makers kept prices un-negotiated, while large employers owed nothing new. Americans without coverage gained nothing from this bill and waited for a different law three years later.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 32 cosponsors were Democrats, roughly one in seven of the chamber's 233 Democrats, and no Republican signed on. Because the bill never reached a vote, opposition was never recorded on a roll call; it died by inaction rather than by a defeat.

industries.note: AmeriCare would become the default insurer for every resident, so private plans survive only as certified employer equivalents, optional Medicare Advantage-style plans inside the program, and tightly regulated supplemental policies with 75-85 percent payout floors, guaranteed renewability, and commission caps. The standalone individual market would effectively disappear.

The Secretary must negotiate purchase prices with manufacturers, pay outpatient drugs by fee schedule, and steer to cheaper therapeutic equivalents — and the negotiation explicitly extends to Medicare Part D, overriding the provision that barred Medicare from negotiating.
Every patient would be insured, cutting uncompensated care, but payment follows Medicare rates and extra billing is banned, so providers would be paid less per case than private insurers pay today.

A new duty to pay at least 80 percent of premium costs for workers on AmeriCare, unless the employer offers an equivalent group plan at the same share; small employers are exempt until 2013. Firms that already fund generous plans are largely unaffected.

industries.industry: Supplemental and Medicare Advantage-style private plans
industries.note: The bill writes a permanent, regulated private role into law: certified AmeriCare supplemental policies with standardized packages and minimum payouts, plus the option to deliver benefits through Medicare Advantage-style health plans. Their market exists only because the public program keeps modest cost-sharing — it grows only if the bill passes.
